name: Facial nerve rehab / neurectomy

lead: Facial nerve paralysis, most often from Bell's palsy, leaves one side of the face weak and visibly asymmetric. Rehabilitation and surgery aim to restore movement so the face is more balanced at rest and in motion.

Drugs reduce nerve inflammation, rehabilitation techniques aim to improve movement, and surgical options include nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers. Neurectomy means cutting selected nerve branches. About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully, and several rehabilitation trials are registered. This is an established clinical field for paralysis, not a studied route for typical faces.

paras: Care usually starts with a diagnosis, then corticosteroids and therapy with exercises, with surgery considered for longer-lasting or severe cases. It is managed by clinicians such as neurologists, therapists and facial plastic surgeons.
Surgical options carry the usual operative risks. Outcomes of neurectomy were not described in the sources reviewed, and paralysis has many causes that need evaluation.

chain: More balanced face at rest and in motion
angle.text: This is the medical route to a more symmetrical face when facial nerve paralysis has caused droop or uneven movement, using therapy, nerve repair, grafting or muscle transfers to restore movement. It is an established clinical field for paralysis patients.

lead: Facial nerve rehabilitation and neurectomy are medical and surgical approaches to facial asymmetry caused by weakness or abnormal movement of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve. Rehabilitation covers therapy and exercise techniques, drugs given early in the course of a palsy, and procedures such as nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers; neurectomy means cutting or removing part of a nerve.[1]

They help someone look better by restoring balance to a face that has dropped, stiffened or moves unevenly after paralysis. When a facial nerve is affected, the smile may pull to one side, the brow may sag, the eye may not close fully and muscles on the unaffected side can look overactive by comparison. Treatment aims to recover movement, reduce abnormal movement, and, where function does not return, rebuild or stand in for it so the face looks more symmetrical at rest and in expression.[1][2]

Facial paralysis has many causes. Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute onset, and others include Lyme disease and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, trauma, tumours, stroke and congenital conditions.[1][3] About 71 percent of people with Bell's palsy are reported to recover fully.[1][3] In looksmaxxing discussion the topic appears as a treatment for paralysis-induced asymmetry rather than as an enhancement for typical faces.

paras: Bell's palsy, of unknown cause but associated with herpes simplex infection, is the most common cause of acute facial paralysis and accounts for about 70 percent of one-sided cases. Other causes include Lyme disease, reactivation of varicella zoster virus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), middle ear infection, temporal bone fractures, acoustic neuromas and parotid tumours, diabetes, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and Moebius syndrome, which is present at birth.[1][3]

Wikipedia reports that Lyme disease accounts for about 25 percent of cases in areas where it is common, and that temporal bone fractures are the most common traumatic cause, with transverse fractures carrying a 40 to 50 percent likelihood of paralysis.[1] Stroke produces a central facial palsy that typically spares the forehead, which is how clinicians tell it apart from a nerve (peripheral) palsy.[1]

Weakness is usually one-sided and may develop over several hours to about 72 hours, sometimes preceded by ear pain. Other features can include loss of taste, sensitivity to sound and reduced tears or saliva.[1][3] Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion: clinicians check which movements are affected, look for forehead sparing, and use imaging or blood tests when trauma, tumour or Lyme disease are suspected.[1][3]

For Bell's palsy, corticosteroids are standard, with antivirals added in severe cases, together with eye protection using artificial tears, ointment and taping during sleep.[1] Corticosteroids begun within three days of onset are reported to improve the chance of recovery, by about 14 percent according to Wikipedia's summary of the evidence.[1][3] A 2015 Cochrane review found no added benefit from antivirals over steroids in mild to moderate disease.[3] A Lancet Neurology trial of prednisolone and valaciclovir is described under clinical studies.[4]

Physiotherapy may help maintain muscle tone and prevent contractures, though Wikipedia notes there is no high-quality evidence for electrical stimulation.[3] Rehabilitation techniques such as Kabat rehabilitation, neural mobilisation, kinesiology taping, photobiomodulation and electrical stimulation are the subject of registered trials in Bell's palsy.[5][6][7][8]
Botulinum toxin is increasingly supported for reducing synkinesis and improving symmetry, according to Wikipedia's Bell's palsy article.[3]

Surgical options described include end-to-end nerve repair after tumour removal, cross-facial nerve grafting, nerve transfers, gracilis free muscle transfer and static procedures that restore symmetry when function does not return.[1] Surgery on the nerve itself is generally not recommended in Bell's palsy; a 2021 Cochrane review could not determine whether early decompression helps or harms.[3]

The surgical anatomy of the face, including the superficial musculo-aponeurotic system (SMAS) described by Mitz and Peyronie in 1976, has been described as relevant to corrective surgery for facial palsy.[2] A registered trial will compare a deep-plane facelift staged with reanimation against reanimation alone for functional and aesthetic outcomes.[9]

After recovery, regenerating nerve fibres can misdirect, so closing the eye may lift the corner of the mouth; Wikipedia reports ongoing problems in about 9 percent of people with Bell's palsy, and other complications include tearing while eating and spasm.[3] Neurectomy in this context generally refers to selectively cutting nerve branches, for example to reduce overactivity on the unaffected or synkinetic side so that the face looks more balanced.

The Persian physician al-Razi (865 to 925) gave the first known description of facial palsy, and the Scottish neurophysiologist Sir Charles Bell (1774 to 1842) described the facial nerve's role, presenting his work to the Royal Society on 12 July 1821; the condition bears his name.[3]

Most people with Bell's palsy begin to recover within three weeks even without treatment; a 1982 study of 1,011 patients reported early recovery in 85 percent and complete recovery in 71 percent after at least a year. Children under 10 tend to fare better and people over 61 worse.[3] In a study of 30 people with stroke-related paralysis, about two-thirds had full recovery or mild paralysis at six months.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial studied prednisolone and valaciclovir in Bell's palsy.[4] Several trials of rehabilitation and physical therapies are registered, including Kabat rehabilitation versus conventional physical therapy (n=36),[5] Kabat versus neural mobilisation (completed, n=28),[8] photobiomodulation for idiopathic facial paralysis (completed, n=96),[6] and photobiomodulation with electrical stimulation (not yet recruiting).[7] A registered trial of deep-plane facelift as a staged adjunct to facial reanimation is also listed.[9] Published outcomes for these registrations have not been reported.
